overview:
On a narrow saddle between two peaks above the Urubamba gorge, some 2,430 metres up on the eastern flank of the Andes, Inca builders laid out roughly two hundred structures of finely fitted dry stone: temples, storehouses, fountains fed by a channelled spring, houses for retainers, and terraces cut into slopes so steep that the whole site reads as an argument with gravity. Most archaeologists take it to have been a royal estate of Pachacuti, the ruler credited with turning Cusco's small polity into the empire the Inca called Tawantinsuyu, built after his campaigns brought the middle and lower Urubamba under Cusco's control. The estate belonged to his lineage rather than to the state, a private retreat and ceremonial precinct rather than a city, and it sat within a network of similar holdings strung along the river. Radiocarbon dates published in 2021 from burials at the site put occupation at roughly 1420 to 1532, pushing the beginning about two decades earlier than the chronology derived from Spanish-era accounts of Pachacuti's reign — a reminder that the tidy regnal dates in colonial sources are themselves reconstructions.

The people who kept the place running were largely yanacona, permanently attached retainers rather than rotational labourers, and the skeletal evidence suggests they were drawn from across the empire: bone chemistry and ancestry point to individuals from the Andean highlands, the Pacific coast, what is now Ecuador, and the Amazonian lowlands, many of them raised on diets characteristic of other regions before they arrived. That mix is a small portrait of how the Inca state moved populations to serve its purposes. When Spanish forces took Cusco in the 1530s the estate lost the court that sustained it, and it appears to have been emptied within a generation. There is no evidence any Spaniard reached it; epidemic disease travelling ahead of the invaders and the collapse of the lineage economy are the usual explanations. The Inca resistance state at Vilcabamba, deeper into the forest, held out until 1572, but Machu Picchu played no recorded part in it.

The site was never wholly forgotten locally — farmers worked its terraces, and Agustín Lizárraga carved his name in the Temple of the Three Windows in 1902 — but it entered international awareness through Hiram Bingham's Yale-backed expedition of 1911 and the publicity he built around it. Bingham also shipped thousands of artefacts north; Yale returned them to Peru only between 2006 and 2012. Even the name is a modern accident: recent work argues the Inca knew the settlement as Huayna Picchu, and that Bingham's publications fixed the neighbouring peak's name to the ruins.
significance: Machu Picchu survives because nobody destroyed it — the Spanish never found it, so its stonework, water channels, terraces and astronomical alignments remain legible in a way almost nothing else Inca does, Cusco itself having been rebuilt as a colonial city on Inca foundations. That accident of preservation makes it the single richest physical text for reading how Inca elites organised landscape, labour and ritual, and it has anchored a century of argument about Andean chronology, about who actually built and inhabited such places, and about the ethics of removing a culture's material past to foreign museums. It also became something its builders never intended: a national symbol for Peru, a UNESCO mixed cultural and natural property since 1983, and one of the most visited archaeological sites on earth, with the crowding and conservation pressure that follows.
coverage: Written from the UNESCO inscription file, reference encyclopaedia entries, and the 2021 Antiquity radiocarbon study; the dataset itself holds no events beneath this story, so nothing here is drawn from the map's own records. The deeper gap is in the record generally: the Inca kept no alphabetic writing, so the estate's purpose, its ceremonies, and even its Inca name are inferred from architecture, burials and Spanish colonial testimony written by and for the conquerors decades after the fact — the attribution to Pachacuti in particular rests on chains of inference that some scholars consider far less settled than popular accounts suggest.
